topics.description: A Babylonian cuneiform artifact recording Cyrus the Great’s conquest of Babylon and policies toward its peoples and temples.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This ruler created a postal system for his empire known as the Chapar Khaneh. Xenophon wrote a biography of this ruler titled for his “education.” This ruler became the only non-Jew to be called “Messiah”nin the Hebrew Bible on account of his victory over Nabonidus. A cuneiform document called the world’s first declaration of (*) human rights was found on a “cylinder” named for this ruler. This founder of Pasargadae conquered the Medes, Lydians, and finally Babylon in 593 BCE, ending the Babylonian captivity. For 10 points, name this “Great” founder of the Achaemenid Empire.
parts.answer: Cyrus the Great [or Cyrus II; accept just Cyrus after “Great” is read]

topics.description: The 312 CE battle in which Constantine defeated Maxentius, an event traditionally associated with Constantine’s conversion to Christianity.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This ruler won the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, uniting two halves of his empire. Just before that battle, this emperor saw the letters “chi” and “ro” in a dream and ordered his men to paint a cross-like symbol on their shields. This ruler was the first Roman emperor to convert to (*) Christianity, and he moved the capital from Rome to a city named after himself. For ten points, name this Roman emperor, the namesake of a city now called Istanbul.

topics.description: Christopher Columbus's 1492–1493 transatlantic expedition reached the Caribbean and initiated sustained European contact and colonization in the Americas.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This event’s denial at the Council of Salamanca was described in a mythologized Washington Irving biography of its leader. Alfred Crosby coined the name for a process began by this event, in which European syphilis rates increased. This event started an “exchange” which saw potatoes enter Europe for the first time. The Niña, Pinta, and Santa Maria were used in, for 10 points, what 1492 event, in which a certain explorer landed in the Americas?
parts.answer: Columbus’ first voyage [accept any answer containing “Christopher Columbus” that describes his journey, or Columbus not-discovering the New World; accept Columbian exchange before “exchange” is mentioned; prompt on answers that do not mention Columbus such as the discovery of the New World]

topics.description: A Saudi journalist and dissident whose 2018 assassination at the Saudi consulate in Istanbul caused international controversy.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: This country’s government planned the construction of the Trojena mountain resort and a 170 kilometer  long linear city in its Neom project. Members of this country’s Tiger Squad potentially carried out the  assassination of dissident journalist Jamal Khashoggi. The initial public offering of (*) Aramco, this country’s  national oil company, was proclaimed by its crown prince, Mohamed bin Salman. For 10 points, name this oil-rich  country governed from Riyadh.

topics.description: The German emperor from 1888 to 1918 who exchanged the “Willy-Nicky” telegrams with Tsar Nicholas II before World War I.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Tsar Nicholas II and this man sent each other a series of ten telegrams in summer 1914 as their countries teetered on the brink of war. For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Nicholas II corresponded with this man, his cousin and the last Kaiser of Germany.
parts.answer: Kaiser Wilhelm II (prompt on “Willy;” prompt on “Wilhelm”)

parts.label: B
parts.question: The “Willy-Nicky” telegrams discussed each one’s fears that the other country was beginning this process of readying troops and supplies for war. This process was seen as an act of war, even though “Willy” and “Nicky” tried to convince each other it was not.

parts.label: C
parts.question: Wilhelm II and Nicholas II were related through - among many, many other royals - this English queen who was known as the “Grandmother of Europe.” This woman’s record as longest-serving British monarch was broken by Elizabeth II.

topics.description: A historic university in Bologna, Italy, founded in 1088 and widely regarded as the oldest continuously operating university in the world.

parts.label: L
parts.question: While at this university, Laura Bassi became the first woman in the world to receive a doctorate in science. For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this Italian university where Bettisia Gozzadini was the first woman in history to receive a degree. This university in Emilia-Romagna is the oldest continuously operating college in the world.
parts.answer: University of Bologna [or UNIBO; or Università di Bologna]

parts.label: B
parts.question: Bassi helped popularize classical mechanics and this idea in Italy. Galileo Galilei was forced by the Church to recant this idea about the Earth’s location in the solar system. A description is acceptable.
parts.answer: heliocentrism [accept answers indicating that the Earth revolves around the Sun or the Sun is at the center of the solar system]

parts.label: C
parts.question: Pope Sixtus IV allowed this kingdom’s Uppsala University to operate under the same hands-off style as the University of Bologna. Rene Descartes died while tutoring this kingdom’s Queen Christina of House Vasa.
parts.answer: Kingdom of Sweden [accept the Swedish Empire]

topics.description: The authoritarian Haitian ruling dynasty formed by François Duvalier and his son Jean-Claude Duvalier, which governed Haiti from 1957 to 1986.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: In 2010, this country’s leader, Rene Preval, escaped without injury when the National Palace collapsed ´ in an earthquake that killed over 100,000 people. In July 2021, over two dozen mercenaries carried out the assassination of (*) Jovenel Mo¨ıse, this country’s president. The Duvalier family led this country as despots for much of the 20th century. The island of Hispaniola is shared by the Dominican Republic and, for ten points, what French-speaking Caribbean nation whose capital is Port-au-Prince?
parts.answer: Haiti (accept Republic of Haiti; accept Repiblik d Ayiti; accept Republique d’ ´ Haiti)

topics.description: The July 14, 1789 attack on Paris’s Bastille prison that became a defining early event of the French Revolution.

parts.label: tossup
parts.question: Two days before this event, a crowd marched to the Tuileries protesting the dismissal of financier Jacques Necker. This violent event followed the signing of the Tennis Court Oath by the Third Estate. Only seven prisoners were actually freed during this event, after which the Jacobin movement was formed. For 10 points, name this July 14, 1789 event in which French revolutionaries stormed a prison in Paris, the inciting incident of the French Revolution.
parts.answer: storming of the Bastille (accept equivalents mentioning an attack on the Bastille; prompt on “French Revolution”)

topics.description: The Ethiopian emperor from 1930 to 1974 who became a central messianic figure in Rastafari belief.

parts.label: L
parts.question: This religion’s adherents follow an ital [“eye”-tahl] diet and believe that western society, or “Babylon,” is harmful to people from Africa, or “Zion.” For ten points each,

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this religion founded in Ethiopia, in which wearing dreadlocks honors the Lion of Judah
parts.answer: Rasta (accept Rastafari; accept word forms like Rastafarianism)

parts.label: B
parts.question: In Rastafari, the Lion of Judah is a symbol of this emperor of Ethiopia, who is sometimes considered the second coming of Jesus.

parts.label: C
parts.question: In Rastafari, grounding ceremonies often incorporate the smoking of this substance, which is valued for its
parts.answer: marijuana (accept ganja; accept synonyms like cannabis; accept slang like pot)

topics.description: An ancient Sumerian city near the mouth of the Euphrates, famous for its Great Ziggurat and the Third Dynasty of Ur.

parts.label: L
parts.question: Amar-Sin (AA-mar-sin), Shu-Sin (SHOO-sin), and Ibbi-Sin (IB-ee-sin) all succeeded a reformer of  this city's Third Dynasty named Shulgi (SHOOL-ghee). For 10 points each:

parts.label: A
parts.question: Name this city near the mouth of the Euphrates (yoo-FRAY-teez), whose Great Ziggurat (ZIG-uh￾raht) was later restored by King Nabonidus (NAA-boh-NAI-dus).
parts.answer: Ur [or Urim; or Uru; do not accept or prompt on “Uruk”]

parts.label: B
parts.question: During Ur's First Dynasty, the city came under control of the Akkadian (ak-AYD-ee-en) Empire,  which was founded by this “Great” first emperor in world history and father of Enheduanna (EN-hed￾WAH-nah).

parts.label: C
parts.question: Ur was an important city-state of Sumer (SOO-mur), which was located in this larger region  between the Tigris (TAI-gris) and Euphrates Rivers where the Babylonian civilization also flourished.
